3.1 UNSIGNED DISCRETIONARY ACCRUALS AND OPERATING VOLATILITY
 We begin by estimating several different discretionary accrual models and
 examining the underlying characteristics of firms in relation to unsigned
 discretionary accrual estimates. Our sample includes all Compustat observations with a minimum of six years of statement of cash flows data, which
 is available on Compustat starting in 1988. We require five years of data
 for our volatility measures, the volatility of operating cash flows (acFo) and
 the volatility of cash revenues (uREv), plus an additional year of data for
 estimating the Dechow-Dichev model. Our final sample consists of 44,469
 firm-year observations from 1994 through 2003. For these firms we compute
 total and current discretionary accruals using the modifiedJones model (denoted MJT and MJC, respectively), discretionary accruals from McNichols's
 [2002] modification to the Dechow-Dichev [2002] model (hereafter, denoted MDD), and performance-matched total discretionary accruals as in
 6 Although the volatility of cash flows could be affected by "real" earnings management, such
 as cuts in research and development or advertising expense, this is not the type of earnings
 management that the models using unsigned discretionary accruals are trying to capture.
